solution: Both numerator and denominator vanish at \(x = 2\), so the factor \((x-2)\) is common. Factorise: \(x^{4}-16 = (x^{2}-4)(x^{2}+4) = (x-2)(x+2)(x^{2}+4)\) and \(x^{2}-5x+6 = (x-2)(x-3)\). Cancelling \((x-2)\), \(\lim_{x \to 2}\frac{(x+2)(x^{2}+4)}{x-3} = \frac{(2+2)(4+4)}{2-3} = \frac{4 \times 8}{-1} = -32\).
why: The surviving denominator \(x-3\) evaluates to \(-1\) at \(x=2\), so the sign is negative.

solution: At \(x = -2\): \((-2)^{7}+128 = -128+128 = 0\) and \((-2)^{3}+8 = -8+8 = 0\), so this is the \(\frac{0}{0}\) form. Write both as differences of like powers about \(a = -2\): \(x^{7}+128 = x^{7}-(-2)^{7}\) and \(x^{3}+8 = x^{3}-(-2)^{3}\). Divide numerator and denominator by \((x-a)\) and use \(\lim_{x \to a}\frac{x^{n}-a^{n}}{x-a} = n\,a^{n-1}\): the limit is \(\frac{7(-2)^{6}}{3(-2)^{2}} = \frac{7 \times 64}{3 \times 4} = \frac{448}{12} = \frac{112}{3}\).
why: \(\frac{7a^{6}}{3a^{2}} = \frac{7}{3}a^{4} = \frac{7}{3}\times 16 = \frac{112}{3}\) with \(a=-2\); the even powers make the result positive.

solution: Each term blows up separately at \(x = 3\), so combine first. \(x^{2}-11x+24 = (x-3)(x-8)\) and \(x^{2}-x-6 = (x-3)(x+2)\). Hence the sum is \(\frac{1}{x-3}\left[\frac{1}{x-8}+\frac{1}{x+2}\right] = \frac{1}{x-3}\cdot\frac{(x+2)+(x-8)}{(x-8)(x+2)} = \frac{1}{x-3}\cdot\frac{2x-6}{(x-8)(x+2)} = \frac{2(x-3)}{(x-3)(x-8)(x+2)} = \frac{2}{(x-8)(x+2)}\). At \(x = 3\) this is \(\frac{2}{(-5)(5)} = -\frac{2}{25}\).
why: The bracket \(\frac{1}{x-8}+\frac{1}{x+2}\) itself contributes a factor \(2(x-3)\), which cancels the singular \(\frac{1}{x-3}\).

solution: As printed, the denominator's radical covers the whole of \(3x-11-2\), i.e. \(\sqrt{3x-13}\). Read that way the denominator tends to \(\sqrt{15-13} = \sqrt{2} \neq 0\) while the numerator tends to \(\sqrt{9}-3 = 0\), so the limit would be \(\frac{0}{\sqrt{2}} = 0\) and NO option is correct. The reading that makes the question a genuine \(\frac{0}{0}\) limit and matches an option is \(\sqrt{3x-11}-2\), the \(-2\) sitting outside the radical. On that reading, rationalise both parts: \(\sqrt{x+4}-3 = \frac{(x+4)-9}{\sqrt{x+4}+3} = \frac{x-5}{\sqrt{x+4}+3}\) and \(\sqrt{3x-11}-2 = \frac{(3x-11)-4}{\sqrt{3x-11}+2} = \frac{3(x-5)}{\sqrt{3x-11}+2}\). The factor \((x-5)\) cancels, leaving \(\lim_{x \to 5}\frac{\sqrt{3x-11}+2}{3\left(\sqrt{x+4}+3\right)} = \frac{2+2}{3(3+3)} = \frac{4}{18} = \frac{2}{9}\).
why: Stem misprint: the radical over-covers. With \(\sqrt{3x-13}\) the limit is \(0\) and no option works; with \(\sqrt{3x-11}-2\) it is \(\frac{2}{9}\).

solution: At \(x = \frac{\pi}{3}\), \(\tan x = \sqrt{3}\) so \(\tan^{2}x - 3 = 0\), and \(\sec x = 2\) so \(\sec^{3}x - 8 = 0\): the \(\frac{0}{0}\) form. Put everything in terms of \(u = \sec x\), using \(\tan^{2}x = \sec^{2}x - 1 = u^{2}-1\). The quotient becomes \(\frac{(u^{2}-1)-3}{u^{3}-8} = \frac{u^{2}-4}{u^{3}-8} = \frac{(u-2)(u+2)}{(u-2)(u^{2}+2u+4)} = \frac{u+2}{u^{2}+2u+4}\). As \(x \to \frac{\pi}{3}\), \(u \to 2\), giving \(\frac{2+2}{4+4+4} = \frac{4}{12} = \frac{1}{3}\).
why: The identity \(\tan^{2}x = \sec^{2}x-1\) turns the whole expression into a single-variable \(\frac{u^{2}-4}{u^{3}-8}\).

solution: Both numerator and denominator tend to \(0\). Divide each by \(x\): the numerator becomes \(5\cdot\frac{\sin x}{x} - \cos x \to 5(1) - 1 = 4\), and the denominator becomes \(2\cdot\frac{\tan x}{x} - 3x \to 2(1) - 0 = 2\). Hence the limit is \(\frac{4}{2} = 2\).
why: Dividing through by \(x\) reduces everything to the standard limits \(\frac{\sin x}{x} \to 1\) and \(\frac{\tan x}{x} \to 1\).

solution: Substitute \(x = \frac{\pi}{2} + h\) so that \(h \to 0\). Then \(\cos x = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+h\right) = -\sin h\) and \(\cos 3x = \cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}+3h\right) = \sin 3h\). The numerator is \(3(-\sin h) + \sin 3h = -3\sin h + \left(3\sin h - 4\sin^{3}h\right) = -4\sin^{3}h\), using \(\sin 3h = 3\sin h - 4\sin^{3}h\). The denominator is \((2x-\pi)^{3} = (2h)^{3} = 8h^{3}\). Hence the limit is \(\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{-4\sin^{3}h}{8h^{3}} = -\frac{4}{8}\left(\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{\sin h}{h}\right)^{3} = -\frac{1}{2}\).
why: The triple-angle expansion cancels the \(3\sin h\) terms exactly, leaving \(-4\sin^{3}h\) over \(8h^{3}\).

solution: Factor the numerator by grouping, using \(15^{x} = 3^{x}5^{x}\): \(15^{x}-3^{x}-5^{x}+1 = 3^{x}5^{x}-3^{x}-5^{x}+1 = 3^{x}(5^{x}-1) - (5^{x}-1) = (3^{x}-1)(5^{x}-1)\). Therefore the expression equals \(\frac{(3^{x}-1)}{x}\cdot\frac{(5^{x}-1)}{x}\cdot\frac{x^{2}}{\sin^{2}x}\). Using \(\lim_{x \to 0}\frac{a^{x}-1}{x} = \log a\) and \(\lim_{x \to 0}\frac{x}{\sin x} = 1\), the limit is \(\log 3 \cdot \log 5\). TWIN: A=B, since \(\log 15 = \log(3 \times 5) = \log 3 + \log 5\), so options A and B are the SAME number written two ways. Both are distractors here (the correct value is the PRODUCT \(\log 3 \cdot \log 5\), not the sum), so the key is unaffected by the duplication.
why: The numerator factors as \((3^{x}-1)(5^{x}-1)\), giving a product of logarithms, not a sum.

solution: This is the \(1^{\infty}\) form. Write the base as \(1\) plus a small quantity: \(\frac{3+5x}{3-4x} = 1 + \frac{(3+5x)-(3-4x)}{3-4x} = 1 + \frac{9x}{3-4x}\). Using \(\lim (1+f)^{g} = e^{\lim fg}\) when \(f \to 0\) and \(fg\) has a finite limit, the exponent is \(\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1}{x}\cdot\frac{9x}{3-4x} = \lim_{x \to 0}\frac{9}{3-4x} = \frac{9}{3} = 3\). Hence the limit is \(e^{3}\).
why: The base exceeds \(1\) by \(\frac{9x}{3-4x}\), so the exponent limit is \(\frac{9}{3} = 3\).

solution: Combine the logarithms: \(\log(5+x)-\log(5-x) = \log\frac{5+x}{5-x} = \log\left(1+\frac{x}{5}\right) - \log\left(1-\frac{x}{5}\right)\). Divide by \(x\) and use \(\lim_{t \to 0}\frac{\log(1+t)}{t} = 1\): \(\frac{\log\left(1+\frac{x}{5}\right)}{x} \to \frac{1}{5}\) and \(\frac{-\log\left(1-\frac{x}{5}\right)}{x} \to \frac{1}{5}\), so the numerator over \(x\) tends to \(\frac{2}{5}\). Since \(\frac{x}{\sin x} \to 1\), the required limit is \(\frac{2}{5}\).
why: Both logarithms contribute \(+\frac{1}{5}\) because the second carries a minus sign inside AND outside.

solution: Put \(t = \frac{\pi}{2}-x\), so \(t \to 0\) and \(\cos x = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-t\right) = \sin t\). The expression becomes \(\frac{3^{\sin t}-1}{t} = \frac{3^{\sin t}-1}{\sin t}\cdot\frac{\sin t}{t}\). As \(t \to 0\), \(\sin t \to 0\), so the first factor tends to \(\log 3\) by \(\lim_{u \to 0}\frac{a^{u}-1}{u} = \log a\), and the second tends to \(1\). Hence the limit is \(\log 3\).
why: The substitution \(t = \frac{\pi}{2}-x\) turns \(\cos x\) into \(\sin t\), matching the standard exponential limit.

solution: Rewrite so that every factor is a standard limit: \(\frac{x\log(1+3x)}{\left(e^{3x}-1\right)^{2}} = \frac{\log(1+3x)}{3x}\cdot\left(\frac{3x}{e^{3x}-1}\right)^{2}\cdot\frac{x \cdot 3x}{(3x)^{2}}\). The first factor tends to \(1\), the squared factor tends to \(1\), and the last is the constant \(\frac{3x^{2}}{9x^{2}} = \frac{1}{3}\). Hence the limit is \(\frac{1}{3}\). (Degree check: the numerator behaves like \(x \cdot 3x = 3x^{2}\) and the denominator like \((3x)^{2} = 9x^{2}\).)
why: Numerator \(\sim 3x^{2}\), denominator \(\sim 9x^{2}\), so the limit is \(\frac{3}{9} = \frac{1}{3}\).

solution: Replace each factor by its standard limit. Numerator: \(\left(3^{\sin x}-1\right)^{3} = \left(\frac{3^{\sin x}-1}{\sin x}\right)^{3}\left(\frac{\sin x}{x}\right)^{3}x^{3}\), which behaves like \((\log 3)^{3}x^{3}\). Denominator: \(3^{x}-1\) behaves like \((\log 3)x\), \(\tan x\) like \(x\), and \(\log(1+x)\) like \(x\), so the product behaves like \((\log 3)x^{3}\). The limit is therefore \(\frac{(\log 3)^{3}}{\log 3} = (\log 3)^{2}\). Note the \(x^{3}\) cancels exactly, confirming the expression is genuinely of \(\frac{0}{0}\) type with a finite non-zero value.
why: Three factors of \(\log 3\) upstairs against one downstairs leaves \((\log 3)^{2}\).

solution: Put \(t = x-3\), so \(t \to 0\) and the expression becomes \(\frac{5^{t}-4^{t}}{\sin t}\). Insert and remove \(1\) in the numerator: \(5^{t}-4^{t} = \left(5^{t}-1\right)-\left(4^{t}-1\right)\). Dividing through by \(t\), \(\frac{5^{t}-1}{t} \to \log 5\) and \(\frac{4^{t}-1}{t} \to \log 4\), while \(\frac{t}{\sin t} \to 1\). Hence the limit is \(\log 5 - \log 4 = \log\frac{5}{4}\).
why: \(\log 5 - \log 4\) is a DIFFERENCE of logs, so it collapses to \(\log\frac{5}{4}\), not to \(\frac{\log 5}{\log 4}\).

solution: The numerator has degree \(7+3 = 10\) and the denominator degree \(10\), so the limit is the ratio of the leading coefficients. Divide numerator and denominator by \(x^{10}\): \(\frac{\left(2+\frac{3}{x}\right)^{7}\left(1-\frac{5}{x}\right)^{3}}{\left(2-\frac{5}{x}\right)^{10}}\). As \(x \to \infty\) each \(\frac{1}{x}\) term vanishes, leaving \(\frac{2^{7}\cdot 1^{3}}{2^{10}} = \frac{128}{1024} = \frac{1}{8}\).
why: Equal degrees, so only the leading coefficients survive: \(\frac{2^{7}}{2^{10}} = 2^{-3} = \frac{1}{8}\).
